description: We are Guardians of the Harvest, a multidisciplinary team from Costa Rica passionate about technology, data, and innovation. Combining skills in software development, analytics, business, and problem-solving, we aim to transform NASA’s Earth observation data into practical solutions for more resilient agriculture.
summary:
Terra Cosmos is a bilingual (English/Spanish) web app that helps smallholder farmers choose crop rotations that protect their soil and cope with a changing climate. A farmer clicks their field on a map and picks the crops they can grow, what they grow now and what matters most: water, soil or climate. The tool ranks two-season rotations for that field, compares them side by side and explains why the current rotation scores lower.

Each crop is scored against the field’s own conditions using NASA Earth observations (NASA POWER climate, SMAP soil moisture, GPM IMERG rainfall), soil maps (pH, texture, organic carbon) and FAO EcoCrop crop requirements. Rotation rules reward legumes and changing plant families and penalize monoculture. To address changing conditions, every sowing is replayed against 26 years of NASA daily weather, El Niño years included, showing how often it would have failed and safer alternatives. Practice cards explain how to build soil health.

This matters because smallholders carry the risk of a failed season alone. Terra Cosmos turns global satellite data into one clear, explainable recommendation per field, so farmers can test resilient options before planting.
details:
Project Link: https://terracosmos.space/app/

What it does. Terra Cosmos is a bilingual (English/Spanish) decision-support web app that helps smallholder farmers choose crop rotations for a specific field. The farmer clicks their field on a map (or tries a one-click demo), picks the crops they can grow, what they grow now and what matters most to them: water, soil or climate. The app ranks two-season rotations with a 0–1 suitability score and a climate/water/soil breakdown, compares the options side by side, and explains in plain language why the farmer’s current rotation scores lower, with the benefits, risks, data behind each score and what the data cannot see.

How it works. Each crop is scored against the field’s own conditions and the crop’s tolerance ranges from FAO EcoCrop: temperature, heat and frost from NASA POWER; rainfall over the crop cycle; root-zone soil moisture and waterlogging from NASA SMAP; and soil pH from OpenLandMap, whose texture and organic carbon maps also inform the waterlogging warnings and soil-health advice. The farmer’s priorities weight the scores, and rotation rules reward legumes and changing plant families while penalizing monoculture. To address changing conditions, every sowing is replayed against up to 26 seasons (2000–2025) of daily NASA GPM IMERG rainfall and MERRA-2 temperature and soil wetness, labeled with NOAA’s El Niño index. The app shows how often each crop would have failed, why, what to do about it and safer alternatives (a different sowing date or another crop). Regenerative practice cards, such as cover crops, legumes and compost, appear only when the field’s data supports them, with the reason for each.

Benefits and impact. Smallholders rarely get field-specific advice on how a changing climate affects their rotations, and they carry the risk of a failed season alone. Terra Cosmos turns free global NASA data into one clear, explainable recommendation per field, compared against what the farmer does today. It is honest about uncertainty: every estimate states its source and resolution, and every result lists what satellites cannot see (drainage, slope, local pests, markets), so farmers and extension officers check locally before acting.

Tools. Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, Pydantic, pandas, httpx, the Google Earth Engine API, an OpenAPI contract checked in CI, pytest (460+ test functions), ruff and mypy. Frontend: React 19, TypeScript and Vite, Leaflet with OpenStreetMap tiles, and hand-drawn SVG charts. Delivery: Docker, GitHub Actions (CI and automatic deploy), Railway hosting and Cloudflare DNS. AI assistants (Claude Code, OpenAI Codex) helped write code, reviewed by the team in pull requests.

Creativity and factors considered. We chose explainability over a black-box score: every number traces back to its NASA source, and the farmer’s own rotation is always the baseline. The past-weather replay with El Niño years turns abstract climate data into a concrete question: would this have worked here in the past 25 years? The demo runs on cached real data, so it works reproducibly. We designed for farmers: plain language, Costa Rican Spanish, a mobile-first layout, keyboard accessibility and color-independent indicators. AI-generated media is labeled, and the agronomic rules and glossary were checked against the backend.
